name: Voltage & Continuity Tester
tagline: The instrument for proving dead — a two-pole tester that shows voltage without a battery.
parts: Two probes — one for each conductor, so the reading comes from the circuit
LED voltage indicators — 12 V steps up to 400 V or 690 V
Polarity indication — shows which side is live
Continuity buzzer and lamp — powered by the instrument's own battery
Single-pole phase test — only ever an indication, never a proof
safety: Proving dead is a sequence, not a poke: test the tester on a known live source, test the circuit, then test the tester on the known source again. A two-pole tester does this properly because it draws its indication from the circuit itself — a single-pole neon screwdriver or a non-contact voltstick is an indication only, and neither is acceptable as proof that a circuit is dead.

points.label: Instrument body
points.detail: A two-pole tester is built for one job and does it in one movement: both probes go on at once, so the voltage it shows comes from the circuit under test rather than from stray capacitance. That is what separates it from a non-contact voltstick, and why it is the accepted way to prove dead.

points.label: LED voltage steps
points.detail: A ladder of LEDs at 12, 50, 120, 230, 400 and sometimes 690 V, lighting together so you read the voltage as a level rather than a number. They work without a battery on most designs — the instrument takes its power from the circuit it is measuring, which is exactly why a flat battery cannot leave you with a false 'dead' reading.

points.label: Continuity and polarity
points.detail: Continuity uses the instrument's own battery to drive a buzzer through the conductor — quick, audible, and the reason it is used for checking protective conductors and bonding before any live test. The same indicators show polarity on DC, and a continuity buzz is how you confirm which conductor is which at the far end of a cable.

points.label: Test / load button
points.detail: Pressing it places a deliberate load across the supply, which pulls down the ghost voltage that a high-impedance meter will happily show on a disconnected conductor running beside a live one. If the reading collapses when you press it, you were looking at induced voltage, not a supply.

points.label: Probes, tips and finger guards
points.detail: GS 38 requires spring-loaded or shrouded tips exposing no more than 4 mm of metal on a probe used near live parts, plus a finger guard so a slip cannot put your hand on the tip. Probes get shorter with use as the tips are replaced — note when they stop springing, because that is when they stop being compliant.

points.label: Lead
points.detail: A single tough lead between the two probes, rated well above the voltage you are testing. Inspect it before use like any other lead: a nick at the strain relief is a failure, not wear.
